subtitulo: Byzantium, religious substitution, and the construction of an identity the nineteenth century would erase (330 – 1204)

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look at

items.text: In Athens, give two hours to the Byzantine and Christian Museum. It is the indispensable complement to the Acropolis, and almost no one visits it: without it, the narrative jumps from the fifth century BC to the nineteenth century AD and produces the illusion of continuity this entry has just dismantled. If you have half a day, visit the monastery of Daphni, with its eleventh-century mosaics, or the one at Kaisariani on Mount Hymettus.

In Corfu, the central object is SAINT SPYRIDON. The saint's relic arrived on the island in 1456, brought from Constantinople by refugees after the fall, and his mummified body is processed four times a year through the old town. It is the heart of Corfiot identity: he is credited with having saved the island from plague and from Ottoman sieges, and an overwhelming proportion of the island's men are named Spiros. Watch who takes part in the procession and who merely watches, how the confraternity is organized, which families hold precedence. It is the best ethnography available on how the cult of a saint organizes a community's memory and hierarchy, and it will be recognizable to anyone who has worked on the Lord of Miracles or an Andean patron-saint feast.

A listening exercise: ask whether anyone still uses the word ROMIÓS or ROMIOSYNI, and in what context. It tends to appear in an affectionate or ironic register, to speak of popular cunning, of getting by, of a plebeian Greekness set against the official one. It is a living fossil of a thousand years of history that nationalism failed to extinguish.

coda.next_hint: The next entry examines the breaking point: 1204, when a Christian crusade sacks Constantinople and Venice seizes the Aegean and the Ionian islands. There begins the specific history of Corfu and Paxos — four Venetian centuries, with no Ottoman conquest — which explains why the islands you are about to visit are, sociologically, another country.

sections.heading: A name no one used
paragraphs: Let us begin with a fact that unsettles almost every reader trained in a Western school: the word BYZANTINE did not exist while Byzantium existed. It was coined by the German scholar Hieronymus Wolf in 1557, more than a century after the fall of Constantinople, and consolidated by French seventeenth-century erudition. The inhabitants of that empire called themselves RHOMAIOI, Romans, and called their state the Basileía tôn Rhōmaíōn, the empire of the Romans. They spoke Greek, prayed in Greek, legislated in Greek from the seventh century onward, and considered themselves Roman without the least contradiction, because "Roman" designated a political and religious belonging, not an ethnicity or a language.

More than that: the word HÉLLĒN, Hellene, meant for centuries "pagan." To call a Christian a Hellene was an insult. The Greek peasant and artisan went on calling themselves ROMIÓS well into the nineteenth century, and the word survives today in popular speech, in songs, and in the expression "romiosyni," which designates a plebeian, long-suffering, cunning Greekness, distinct from and at times opposed to the classical Hellenism of the elites. When, in the nineteenth century, the new national state decided that Greeks descended from Pericles and not from the subjects of the emperor of Constantinople, it had to re-educate its own population to stop calling itself what it had always called itself.

Hold on to this, because it dismantles at a stroke the illusion of continuity. Modern Greek national identity is not the natural persistence of a three-thousand-year essence: it is a deliberate nineteenth-century construction that selected one past — the classical one —, subordinated another — the Byzantine one —, and repressed a third — the Ottoman one. Every national identity works this way. Recognizing it in Greece makes it easier to recognize in Peru, where the nineteenth-century republican project glorified the Inca, cornered the colonial past as a source of shame, and rendered the living indigenous person invisible, with the consequences that Flores Galindo and Cotler described.

sections.heading: Religious substitution as a technology of power
paragraphs: Constantine refounds Byzantium as Constantinople in AD 330, and Christianity passes, in less than a century, from persecuted sect to exclusive state religion — Theodosius imposes it in 380 and bans pagan cults in 392. The process was not a gentle conversion of consciences. It was an operation of material substitution over the landscape: temples were closed, plundered, or converted. The Parthenon becomes a church of the Virgin around the sixth century. The oracle of Delphi falls silent. In 529 Justinian orders the closure of the philosophical schools of Athens, ending nine hundred years of Platonic teaching; the last Neoplatonic philosophers emigrate to Persia.

The technique — occupying the sacred building of the defeated and consecrating it to one's own cult — is proven effective, because it does not destroy the prestige of the place but inherits it. And it is exactly the same technique applied in Cusco a thousand years later: the Coricancha, the Temple of the Sun, still holds up the walls of the convent of Santo Domingo, and the superposition is visible to the naked eye, Inca ashlar below, colonial arch above. When you stand before the Parthenon, remember that it was a temple of Athena, a Christian church, an Ottoman mosque, and a powder magazine, and that its current state — bare columns, no roof, without the Christian and Muslim layers, carefully removed by nineteenth- and twentieth-century archaeologists — is not its natural state but A POLITICAL CHOICE OF THE NINETEENTH CENTURY: Greece decided that its monument had to look classical, and erased fifteen hundred years of its own history from the building. Restoration is always a thesis about which past deserves to exist.

sections.heading: The most bureaucratic state of the Middle Ages
paragraphs: While the Latin West fragmented into lordships, Byzantium preserved and perfected what Western Europe lost: a state. Monetized taxation and a land registry, a paid army, a stable currency — the gold solidus kept its standard for nearly seven hundred years, something without equivalent in monetary history —, a law codified in Justinian's Corpus Iuris between 529 and 534 that would found the whole subsequent European legal tradition, and a professional diplomacy that treated war as the most expensive and least desirable resource. Byzantine military treatises explicitly recommend buying, dividing, and bribing before fighting. Hence, incidentally, the modern pejorative use of "Byzantine" to designate excessive subtlety: Western contempt for a political culture that preferred negotiation to confrontation.

From the seventh century onward the empire reorganizes into THEMES, provinces where military and civil command are unified and where soldiers receive land in exchange for hereditary service. It is an emergency solution against the Arab conquests — Syria, Egypt, and North Africa are lost between 636 and 698 — and it works for three centuries. Its subsequent erosion, as the landed aristocracy absorbs the plots of the soldier-farmers, reproduces with exactness what we saw in Sparta: the state weakens when the concentration of land destroys the class that militarily sustained it. The Macedonian emperors legislated against the DYNATOI, the powerful, throughout the tenth century, and lost.

The iconoclastic crisis — between 726 and 843, with an interval — is usually presented as a theological dispute over the licitness of images. It was also a conflict over the control of resources and of symbolic authority: the monasteries, owners of tax-exempt land and producers of icons, against an imperial power seeking to discipline them. The final victory of the iconodules in 843 — still celebrated today as the "Triumph of Orthodoxy" — consolidated the Church as an autonomous patrimonial power. It is a direct precedent for the role the Orthodox Church would play under Ottoman rule, and one it still retains in the Greece of 2026.

sections.heading: Fallmerayer, or how genetics is used against a nation
paragraphs: Between the sixth and eighth centuries, Slavic populations settled widely across the Balkans and the Peloponnese; the empire gradually reintegrated them through Christianization and administration. It is a well-documented archaeological and toponymic fact — there are Slavic place names throughout the Peloponnese — and in itself banal: every European population is the product of successive mixtures.

But in 1830, the very year the great powers recognized Greek independence, the Tyrolean historian Jakob Philipp Fallmerayer published the thesis that "not one drop of authentic Hellenic blood flows in the veins of the Christian population of present-day Greece," that modern Greeks were Hellenized Slavs and Albanians. The thesis, scientifically untenable in its absolute formulation, had a devastating and deliberate political effect: if modern Greeks did not descend from the ancients, then the European philhellenism that had financed their independence lacked foundation, and Greek territorial claims against the Ottoman Empire — which Russia and Austria opposed for reasons of balance — lost legitimacy. Fallmerayer was writing in a precise geopolitical context, not in a scholarly vacuum.

The Greek reaction was equally political: the national historiography of Konstantinos Paparrigopoulos built, from 1860 onward, the scheme of tripartite continuity — ancient Greece, Byzantium, modern Greece — that rehabilitated the Byzantine empire as a necessary link and that is still taught in Greek schools. That is to say: Byzantium was reincorporated into the national narrative not out of historiographical conviction but as a response to an external attack. The entire architecture of modern Greek identity was built under fire.

The Peruvian parallel is precise and worth stating without evasion: racial arguments about the degeneration or incapacity of Andean populations circulated in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with the same political function — delegitimizing the capacity for self-government — and produced symmetrically nationalist responses. The Fallmerayer debate and the debate over Lima's scientific racism are the same debate: who has the right to claim a past, and what is granted or denied in the present on the basis of that answer.

sections.heading: The Ionian islands, Venice, and the fatal chrysobull of 1082
paragraphs: The Ionian islands were, throughout this entire period, a military frontier. Organized into the theme of Cephalonia around the eighth century, they served as a shield against Arab attacks from Sicily and, above all, against the Normans. Robert Guiscard besieged Corfu and Durazzo between 1081 and 1085 with the declared aim of reaching Constantinople, and died on Cephalonia in 1085.

To resist that offensive, Emperor Alexios I Komnenos did what states without a sufficient fleet do: he hired one. The price was the chrysobull of 1082, which granted Venice total exemption from tariffs throughout the empire and its own quarter in Constantinople. It is, probably, the most costly commercial concession in medieval history. Within a century, Venetian merchants — and later Genoese and Pisan ones — controlled the empire's maritime trade, paying lower taxes than the Byzantine subjects themselves, who were left at a competitive disadvantage within their own market. Later attempts to reverse the concession provoked reprisals and culminated in episodes of violence, including the massacre of the Latins in Constantinople in 1182 and Venice's response to it.

This mechanism — granting fiscal and commercial advantages to an outside actor in exchange for security or immediate credit, and discovering decades later that one's own economy has been alienated — is one of the most recurring patterns in the history of peripheries, and it has a modern technical name: CAPITULATIONS. We will see it again in the nineteenth-century Ottoman Empire, in the Greek debt of 1893, and in contemporary forms such as the tax-stability clauses of Peruvian mining contracts or the conditions of the Greek memoranda of 2010–2015. The structure is identical: an urgent need is paid for with a permanent renunciation. And the road from 1082 to 1204 is, to a large degree, the deferred execution of that debt.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: Islam, the Tang, Wari
paragraphs: The period covered by this entry is the one of greatest global reconfiguration in the whole of the Middle Ages. The Islamic expansion, beginning in 632, tears two-thirds of its territory away from Byzantium in sixty years and creates a civilization that, between the eighth and twelfth centuries, is the most advanced on the planet in mathematics, medicine, optics, and astronomy, and that preserves and comments on the Greek philosophical corpus that the West had lost: Aristotle returns to Europe in the thirteenth century translated from Arabic. Tang and later Song China produces printing, paper money, and a meritocratic bureaucracy chosen by examination. The Carolingians build, in the West, a comparatively rudimentary empire.

In the Andes, between the seventh and eleventh centuries, Wari and Tiwanaku establish the first administrations of truly imperial scale: a road network, standardized state architecture, productive colonies across distinct ecological tiers, control of reciprocity. Wari is, strictly speaking, the laboratory from which Tahuantinsuyo will emerge, just as the theme system is the laboratory of the provincial administration that sustained Byzantium. Both collapse around the year 1000 and give way to regional states — Chimú, Chincha on one side; the world of the Komnenian lordships and local powers on the other. The simultaneity is remarkable and is rarely taught.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: the Church as an institution of state
paragraphs: The most living Byzantine legacy in present-day Greece is not architectural but institutional. The Greek Constitution recognizes the Orthodox Church as the "prevailing religion"; the clergy are paid out of the public budget under a historical agreement over expropriated Church property; religious instruction is an ordinary subject in public schools. Attempts at separation — the 2018 bill under the Syriza government — failed.

Two recent events show the ongoing force of the conflict. In February 2024, Greece approved civil marriage equality, becoming the first majority-Orthodox country to do so; the law passed with opposition votes and against the outright opposition of the Holy Synod, which denounced it from the pulpit. And on the geopolitical plane, the granting of autocephaly to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine by the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople in 2019 caused a rupture in communion with the Patriarchate of Moscow and turned a canonical dispute into one more front of the war that began in 2022. Orthodoxy is not folklore: it is a transnational structure with the capacity for political alignment, and Constantinople — today Istanbul, with a patriarchate of barely a few thousand local faithful and jurisdiction over millions — remains its disputed symbolic center.

The Peruvian mirror is direct. The 1993 Constitution recognizes the Catholic Church as an "important element in the historical, cultural, and moral formation of Peru," and the 1980 Agreement with the Holy See maintains fiscal privileges and a presence in public education. The conservative mobilization of 2016–2017 around gender ideology in the school curriculum, and the subsequent debates over civil unions and reproductive rights, reproduce the same equation: a religious institution with a privileged legal position acting as a veto over the legislative agenda. The difference is that in Greece religion is, in addition, fused with the definition of the nation — it was the Church that preserved identity under Ottoman rule, as we shall see in the next entry —, which makes separation far harder even to propose.
